title: Two Hours of Weights a Week Cut Dementia Death Risk by 27 Per Cent. Most South Asians Are Not Lifting.
excerpt: A Harvard study of 147,000 adults over 30 years found that combining resistance training with cardio slashed all-cause mortality by 45 per cent. The diaspora's favourite exercise — walking — is not enough on its own.
body:
The advice desi families pass down about exercise tends to sound the same everywhere: go for a walk after dinner, do some yoga in the morning, maybe join a badminton group on weekends. Rarely does anyone mention picking up a barbell. A landmark study from Harvard now suggests that omission could be costing South Asians years of healthy life.

Researchers at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health analysed data from 147,374 adults tracked over up to 30 years — one of the longest and largest studies ever conducted on resistance training and mortality. Their findings, published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, are unambiguous: people who performed between 90 and 119 minutes of resistance training per week had a 13 per cent lower risk of dying from any cause compared to those who did none.

The numbers get sharper when broken down by cause of death. The same group experienced a 19 per cent lower risk of death from cardiovascular disease and a 27 per cent reduction in death from neurological diseases — the vast majority of which were dementia-related.

## The Combination That Changes Everything

The most striking finding was not about weights alone. Adults who combined resistance training with regular aerobic exercise — running, cycling, swimming, or brisk walking — saw up to a 45 per cent lower risk of death compared to sedentary individuals. That is not a marginal improvement. That is nearly half the mortality risk wiped away by two types of movement done consistently.

Crucially, more was not always better. The study found no additional reduction in mortality risk beyond approximately 120 minutes of resistance training per week. Two hours, spread across three or four sessions, appears to be the sweet spot.

"The conversation about longevity often focuses on living longer, but I believe the more important goal is maintaining the strength, mobility, independence, and vitality to fully participate in life as we age," said Josephine Hunt, an educational leader and former group fitness instructor who was not involved in the study.

## Why This Matters for South Asians

South Asians carry a disproportionate burden of the very conditions that resistance training most effectively combats. A major study published earlier this year in the Journal of the American Heart Association found that South Asian men had a 31 per cent prevalence of prediabetes by age 45 — compared to just 4 per cent among white men. Hypertension, dyslipidemia, and Type 2 diabetes all emerge earlier and hit harder in the diaspora.

Resistance training directly addresses these metabolic risks. It improves insulin sensitivity, reduces visceral fat, lowers resting blood pressure, and builds the lean muscle mass that serves as a metabolic engine for glucose disposal. Yet South Asians remain dramatically underrepresented in strength training. Cultural preferences lean heavily toward walking and yoga — both valuable but insufficient on their own.

The problem compounds with age. After 40, adults lose roughly 3 to 8 per cent of muscle mass per decade, a process called sarcopenia that accelerates after 60. For South Asians, who already face earlier onset of metabolic disease, the loss of protective muscle mass creates a compounding vulnerability that no amount of evening walks can offset.

## What the Diaspora Should Actually Do

The study's practical implications are straightforward. Hunt, the fitness professional, emphasised that resistance training does not mean bodybuilding or heavy powerlifting. "It is about preserving the ability to live life on your own terms," she said. Dumbbells, resistance bands, bodyweight exercises like squats and push-ups, and machine-based training all count.

For women, the data is especially compelling. Muscle mass and bone density decline more rapidly after menopause, making resistance training not optional but essential for long-term independence. The study's authors noted that the benefits applied across age groups and were not limited to those who started young.

The research does carry limitations. It relied on self-reported exercise data and drew primarily from white, middle-aged health professionals, which means the exact percentages may differ for South Asian populations. But the direction of the evidence is overwhelming, and it aligns with decades of smaller studies showing that muscle-strengthening activity reduces all-cause mortality independently of aerobic fitness.

For a community that has embraced 10,000 daily steps as the gold standard of health, the message from Harvard is clear: walking is a floor, not a ceiling. Pick up the weights.
